hook.text: An interval needs just two numbers: an estimate, and its standard error.

users.text: Fifty users spend an average of forty-nine dollars twenty-eight a month. That's the estimate.

wobble.text: Another fifty would average something else, and the standard error says by how much: about a dollar fifty.

margin.text: Multiply it by a critical value, two point oh one, and you get the margin of error: three dollars and six cents.

interval.text: Step that far either way, and the interval runs from forty-six twenty-two to fifty-two thirty-three.

why.text: Why not the usual one point nine six? The spread was estimated from the same fifty people, and the t-distribution widens the band a little to pay for that.

means-in.text: Building one is easy. Saying what it means is where people slip.

coverage.text: So play god for a moment. Here's a population whose true mean you know: a hundred.

draw.text: Draw forty values, build an interval... then do it again, a hundred times.

hits.text: Ninety-four intervals catch the true mean. Six miss it.

unlucky.text: The misses used the same correct recipe. They just drew unlucky samples.

recipe.text: So the ninety-five percent describes the recipe: run it again and again, and about ninety-five in a hundred catch the truth.

yours.text: Your interval is just ONE of these lines. It holds the truth or it doesn't... and you can't see which.

wrong-in.text: That's the sentence almost everyone gets wrong.

misread.text: The usual version: there's a ninety-five percent chance the true mean is in this interval.

fixed.text: But the true mean never moves. Once your interval is drawn, nothing is random any more. It's in, or it's out.

data.text: Another misreading: ninety-five percent of the data falls inside. Back to the fifty users.

eleven.text: Only eleven of the fifty spend inside it. The interval pins down their average, not any one person.

safer.text: And a wider interval isn't safer. It's just less precise.

wide.text: So what makes an interval wide? Three things.

level.text: First, the confidence you ask for. Take one sample of two hundred, and build its interval at eighty, ninety, ninety-five and ninety-nine percent.

costs.text: Each is wider than the last, from two point one to four point two five. More confidence costs precision.

size.text: Second, the sample size. Hold the level at ninety-five, and grow the sample from twenty-five to sixteen hundred.

halves.text: Each time the data quadruples, the width roughly halves: eleven, five, two point three, one point two.

noise.text: And third, the spread of the data. Double it, and the width doubles too.

rate-in.text: The same recipe works for a rate.

rate.text: Say five hundred and forty of three thousand visitors convert. That's eighteen percent.

rate-se.text: A rate's standard error comes from the rate itself, and here it's seven tenths of a point.

rate-ci.text: Step one point nine six of those either way, and you get sixteen point six to nineteen point four percent.

test-in.text: And an interval can answer a question you might think needs a test.

test.text: Build an interval for a difference. If it leaves out zero, the difference is significant at the five percent level.

straddle.text: This one runs from minus a half to eight. It includes zero, so you can't rule out no effect.

eight.text: But it includes eight as well, a big effect you can't rule out either. That isn't proof of nothing. It's a call for more data.

views.text: An interval and a test are two views of one thing, and only the interval shows how big the effect might be.

formula-in.text: Every interval so far leaned on a formula for the standard error.

bootstrap.text: [curious] But what's the standard error of a median? Or a correlation? The formula is ugly, or doesn't exist.

trick.text: The bootstrap's answer is bold: treat your sample as if it were the population.

waits.text: Here are sixty customer wait times, skewed, not normal.

resample.text: Draw sixty from them, with replacement. Some come up twice, or three times... and some not at all.

again.text: Average that resample. Then do it all again, five thousand times.

pile.text: The averages pile up into a bootstrap distribution. Its spread is the standard error, zero point four eight, where the formula says zero point four nine.

middle.text: And its middle ninety-five percent, six point one to eight point oh, is almost exactly the t-interval.

payoff-in.text: For a mean, that's the long way round. The payoff is everything else.

median.text: Take a hundred and twenty incomes, skewed enough that the median is the honest summary.

word.text: Run the same loop, and change one word: median, instead of mean.

lumpy.text: The medians pile up a little lumpy, because a median can only land near values you actually saw.

range.text: Their middle ninety-five percent runs from about thirty thousand eight hundred to thirty-seven thousand one hundred. No formula needed.

limits.text: But the bootstrap can't create information. It only reuses the data you have.

biased.text: Resample a biased sample, and every resample carries the bias: a confident interval... around the wrong center.

edge.text: And it fails at the edges. A resample can never beat the largest value you saw, so it can't say much about a maximum.

precision.text: It measures how much an estimate wobbles, not whether it's aimed at the truth.

next.text: So an interval says which values are plausible. A test asks about one value in particular... could the effect be zero?
